<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-flaxseeds" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-flaxseeds-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of flaxseeds, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Flaxseeds, as sold; As sold, as eaten or fresh weight, µg/kg; no moisture conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>≤17.6</td><td>≤50</td><td>10–50 (bounded)</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>≤20</td><td>≤50</td><td>5–50 (bounded)</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>53 reference units; 1 sampling family. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>53</td><td>100%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for flaxseeds, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>WHO GEMS/Food is the only compatible sampling family for flaxseeds, as sold on this basis in the completed flaxseeds ledger, so this single-family reference cannot represent other markets. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" class="internal" data-slug="sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" data-no-cite-meta>WHO GEMS/Food</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. Method: hmi-pooled-reference-v2.</p><p>hmi-pooled-reference-v2:flaxseeds-5e925f95cecb:45db230514fb</p><p>The reference is computed by HMI from admitted evidence, not copied from a study baseline. It describes the evidence currently in this scope; it is not a worldwide or current-lot benchmark. Source, year and region filters do not change it. Different HMI scopes are not one common ranking.</p></details></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:flaxseeds-d07b1fbb9f04:1a73a112a5da"><summary>HMI flaxseeds Pb reference · Flaxseeds, as sold, dry weight</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:flaxseeds-d07b1fbb9f04:1a73a112a5da"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI flaxseeds Pb reference · Flaxseeds, as sold, dry weight. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach flaxseeds

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach flaxseeds comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Flaxseeds, oil from pressed raw oil, fraction 1, one production lot had Fe higher at 2,460 µg/kg, against 270 µg/kg for extraction in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2016</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">A comparative study of the content of heavy metals in oils:</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, flaxseeds, as sold from conventional flaxseeds (production system) had chromium higher at 249 µg/kg, against 113 µg/kg for organic flaxseeds (production system) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Brum RdL, Siedzik K, Alejandro-Vega S, Paz-Montelongo S, Gutiérrez-Fernández AJ, González-Weller D, Hardisson A, Misniakiewicz M, Pyrzyńska E, da Silva Júnior FMR, Rubio C · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional">Assessment of Essential Elements and Potentially Toxic Elements (PTEs) in Organic and Conventional Flaxseeds: Implications for Dietary Exposure and Food Safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

and 50 µg/kg (upper quartile).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health <a id="trade-offs-and-failure-modes"></a>
## Trade-offs and limits of controls

<a id="hmi-ing-022"></a>
<a id="can-an-intervention-increase-another-contaminant-or-redistribute-contamination-to-a-by-product"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-023"></a>

<a id="hmi-ing-024"></a>
<a id="what-costs-constraints-adverse-effects-or-failure-modes-are-documented-and-which-are-unknown"></a>

Avoiding exposed growing areas lowered the metal measured in the studies available, but no study measured the cost or supply effect of doing so.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2016</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">A comparative study of the content of heavy metals in oils:</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.

A useful lot result names the form, the basis and a quantification limit well below the limit that applies.

<a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Flaxseeds FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-flaxseeds" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-flaxseeds" data-question="What heavy metals are found in flaxseeds?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in flaxseeds?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, total mercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, B, Ba, Ca, K, Li, Mg, Mo, Na and Sr in flaxseeds, most often lead, cadmium and total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2016</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">A comparative study of the content of heavy metals in oils:</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/lee2019-food-processing-heavy-metals-migration|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Lee JG, Hwang JY, Lee HE, Kim TH, Choi JD, Gang GJ · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/lee2019-food-processing-heavy-metals-migration">Effects of food processing methods on migration of heavy metals to food</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Biological Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/lee2019-food-processing-heavy-metals-migration">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Brum RdL, Siedzik K, Alejandro-Vega S, Paz-Montelongo S, Gutiérrez-Fernández AJ, González-Weller D, Hardisson A, Misniakiewicz M, Pyrzyńska E, da Silva Júnior FMR, Rubio C · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional">Assessment of Essential Elements and Potentially Toxic Elements (PTEs) in Organic and Conventional Flaxseeds: Implications for Dietary Exposure and Food Safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> WHO GEMS/Food submissions reported lead in flaxseeds, as sold from 1,648 results in 3 reporting regions, with subgroup medians below 95 µg/kg, mostly non-detects.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-flaxseeds" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-flaxseeds" data-question="How do heavy metals get into flaxseeds?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into flaxseeds?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, flaxseeds from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than flaxseeds from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Brum RdL, Siedzik K, Alejandro-Vega S, Paz-Montelongo S, Gutiérrez-Fernández AJ, González-Weller D, Hardisson A, Misniakiewicz M, Pyrzyńska E, da Silva Júnior FMR, Rubio C · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional">Assessment of Essential Elements and Potentially Toxic Elements (PTEs) in Organic and Conventional Flaxseeds: Implications for Dietary Exposure and Food Safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Flaxseeds, as sold from organic flaxseeds (production system) had lead higher at 368 µg/kg, against 286 µg/kg for conventional flaxseeds (production system) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Brum RdL, Siedzik K, Alejandro-Vega S, Paz-Montelongo S, Gutiérrez-Fernández AJ, González-Weller D, Hardisson A, Misniakiewicz M, Pyrzyńska E, da Silva Júnior FMR, Rubio C · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional">Assessment of Essential Elements and Potentially Toxic Elements (PTEs) in Organic and Conventional Flaxseeds: Implications for Dietary Exposure and Food Safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/brum2025-flaxseeds-ptes-organic-conventional">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-flaxseeds" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-flaxseeds" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in flaxseeds?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in flaxseeds?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, flaxseeds, as sold had the lowest cadmium subgroup median in EURO (120 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (418 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-flaxseeds-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-flaxseeds-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in flaxseeds is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in flaxseeds is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 3 results from 2 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2014 reported inorganic arsenic at 20.8 µg/kg (mean) in flaxseeds, as sold from European dietary-survey occurrence data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
